summary: Specifies how to find which Registration Data Access Protocol server is authoritative for a query, such as a domain name, IP address, or autonomous system number. It is an Internet Standard and obsoletes RFC 7484.

plainLanguage.summary: RDAP defines how to ask for registration data, but clients also need to know which server to contact. RFC 9224 defines IANA-hosted registries that map domains, IP address ranges and AS numbers to RDAP service URLs.

subtitle: How an RDAP client finds which registration-data server to query for a domain, address or AS number.

tldr.problem: RDAP specifications define how to query registration data but do not say which server is authoritative for a domain, IP address or Autonomous System number.
tldr.mechanism: IANA publishes JSON bootstrap registries for domain names, IPv4, IPv6 and AS-number ranges. A client matches its query to an entry, selects a base RDAP URL and appends the query path.
tldr.outcome: Clients can find the authoritative RDAP service using IANA-maintained delegation data. RFC 9224 is an Internet Standard that obsoletes RFC 7484.

facts.label: Registry sets
facts.value: Domain names, IPv4, IPv6 and AS numbers

today: RFC 9224 is an Internet Standard (STD 95) that obsoletes RFC 7484. Its changes are minor clarifications, with no substantive change to the method.

sections.title: Finding the Authoritative RDAP Server
sections.content:
The Registration Data Access Protocol (RDAP) defines queries and responses for registration data, but its query specifications do not identify the server for each requested domain, address or Autonomous System (AS) number.

These objects are delegated through registries whose data and processes are already maintained by IANA. RFC 9224 defines JSON RDAP Bootstrap Service Registries based on those allocation registries. A client downloads the registry, matches its query and uses the associated base URL.
sections.plainLanguage: RDAP explains how to ask a registry a question but not which registry to ask. The bootstrap registries connect a query to its authoritative service.

sections.title: The JSON Registry Structure
sections.content:
Each registry is a JSON object with a version, publication timestamp, optional description and services array. Each service entry contains two arrays: the entries it covers and the base RDAP URLs for those entries. The arrays are not ordered.

A base RDAP URL must end with a slash because the client appends the query path defined by RFC 9082. If both HTTPS and HTTP URLs are listed, clients should prefer HTTPS. Clients must ignore unrecognized JSON properties and values. Domain labels are lowercase, and internationalized labels appear in A-label form.
sections.plainLanguage: Each registry groups the names or ranges served by a set of RDAP URLs. The client appends the requested query path to one of those base URLs.

sections.title: Matching Domains, IP Addresses and AS Numbers
sections.content:
For domain names, the client compares labels from right to left and uses the longest label-wise match. If a query for a.b.example.com matches both com and example.com, the more specific example.com entry wins. Matching is by label, not by character sequence.

For IPv4 and IPv6, the client selects the longest matching address prefix, comparing address bits up to each prefix length. This lets a broad prefix point to one service while a more specific prefix uses another. IPv4 entries use CIDR notation, and IPv6 entries use the recommended text representation in RFC 5952.

AS-number entries are inclusive ranges in increasing decimal order, with a single number represented by the same number at both ends. Ranges must not overlap. If a service lists several URLs and one does not answer, the client can try another.
sections.plainLanguage: The client chooses the most specific matching domain label or address prefix. For AS numbers, it chooses the range containing the requested number.

sections.title: Caching and Limits
sections.content:
Clients should cache the IANA registries rather than downloading them for every RDAP query. HTTP signaling such as the Expires header can tell a client when to refresh its cache.

A newly allocated domain, address range or AS range may not yet appear in a bootstrap registry because its RDAP service may not be ready. If an entry is missing, the client has no known server and should give the user an appropriate error. This method also does not locate authoritative servers for entity handles, nameserver queries, help requests or search patterns without a matching terminating string.
sections.plainLanguage: Clients keep a local copy of the registries and refresh it when needed. A new registration may not have an RDAP service entry yet, and this method does not cover every type of RDAP query.

sections.title: Security and IANA Requirements
sections.content:
The bootstrap method helps clients obtain registration data from an authoritative server rather than a rogue source. The registries themselves must be available only through HTTPS, and their JSON responses must use the application/json media type.

IANA builds the registries from its existing allocation data plus RDAP server information. The RFC does not alter the allocation policies. Because client software may download these registries frequently, clients should use caching and HTTP expiry information to avoid unnecessary load.
sections.plainLanguage: Clients use protected HTTPS connections to retrieve the IANA registry and then locate the listed service. Caching reduces repeated downloads.
